title: Tyler’s District 1 Ballot Deadline Is Monday. Here’s What Candidates and Voters Should Know
summary: Tyler’s special election to fill the District 1 City Council seat is set for Nov. 3, and regular candidates have until 5 p.m. Monday, Aug. 17, to file. The city’s public candidate list was still blank Friday morning.
content:
Tyler is three days away from a consequential deadline in a local race that has received far less attention than the statewide and congressional contests sharing the Nov. 3 ballot. Anyone seeking a regular place on the ballot for the city’s District 1 special election must file by 5 p.m. Monday, Aug. 17.

The election will fill the City Council seat Stuart Hene left when he became mayor. The city’s official biography says Hene served District 1 from 2021 until his election as mayor on June 13, 2026. He was sworn in after the runoff, creating the vacancy the special election is designed to fill.

Tyler’s election page identifies the contest as the Nov. 3 special election for City Council District 1. As of Friday morning, Aug. 14, the candidate-information section beneath that heading did not list a candidate. That does not prove nobody has submitted paperwork: websites can lag behind filings, and a campaign-finance document is not the same as an accepted ballot application. The city clerk should publish each accepted application and update the roster promptly as the deadline passes.

For a regular candidate, the Texas secretary of state’s 2026 calendar sets 5 p.m. Aug. 17 as the filing deadline for local political subdivisions using the Nov. 3 uniform election date. Tyler’s calendar lists the same day. The city says the deadline for a declaration of write-in candidacy is Friday, Aug. 21. Those are different filing paths, and prospective candidates should use the correct form rather than relying on a social-media announcement.

Applications go through the Tyler city clerk. The city lists City Hall at 212 N. Bonner Ave. and regular office hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Candidates should confirm receipt before the deadline and keep a copy of every filed document. A campaign launch, treasurer appointment or finance report does not by itself place a name on the ballot.

The city charter qualifications posted by Tyler require a council candidate to be a qualified voter, to have lived in the district for at least six months before the election and to continue living in the district while representing it. Prospective candidates should verify the district boundary and their registration before filing. The city’s online district tool and clerk’s office can help resolve address questions.

This is a district seat, not an at-large vote. Only eligible voters who reside in Tyler City Council District 1 will choose the replacement. District labels used for Congress, the Legislature, county precincts and school boards are separate; a voter should confirm the municipal district attached to the home address.

The Nov. 3 election will run alongside major federal and state races, which can help turnout but also bury a local contest near the bottom of a long ballot. The council member elected from District 1 will vote on Tyler’s budget, tax rate, public safety, streets, water and sewer work, zoning and appointments. Those decisions are close to home even when the race receives less advertising.

Voters should expect basic disclosures from every candidate who qualifies. A useful opening questionnaire would ask why the person is running, which neighborhoods are inside District 1, what service problem should be addressed first, how the candidate would evaluate tax and utility proposals, and which financial or organizational interests could create conflicts. Answers should be specific enough to check later.

Campaign-finance transparency also matters in a short special-election cycle. Tyler’s election page already serves as a repository for reports by officeholders and potential candidates. The city should distinguish appointment-of-treasurer forms, periodic finance reports and accepted ballot applications so residents do not have to infer status from a filename. Candidates should disclose donors, expenditures and outstanding obligations on the schedule required by law.

The city lists early voting from Oct. 19 through Oct. 30, including weekend hours, with Election Day voting from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3. Because locations and eligibility details may change, voters should use Tyler and Smith County election pages for the final notice rather than an old sample ballot or shared screenshot.

The Texas secretary of state has designated Dec. 12 for runoffs produced by Nov. 3 local elections. Whether Tyler needs one will depend on the certified candidate field and results. The city should state the threshold and runoff procedure clearly when it publishes the final ballot.

Hene’s move from District 1 to the mayor’s office is not, by itself, a mandate for any particular successor. The special election gives district residents a fresh choice. Candidates can respect the outgoing council member’s record while explaining where they would agree, where they would differ and how they would independently review city business.

Monday’s deadline is therefore more than paperwork. It determines which regular candidates voters will be able to compare in the months ahead. Tyler should post the accepted field, filing documents and election order quickly after 5 p.m.; candidates should make their priorities and finances easy to inspect; and District 1 residents should put the local race on the same checklist as the better-known contests above it.
